top1_chunks.title: Johnson & Johnson Announces Updated Financials and 2023 Guidance Following Completion of the Kenvue Separation - Introduction
top1_chunks.summary: Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) announced updated 2023 guidance following completion of the Kenvue separation, repositioning J&J as a Pharmaceutical and MedTech company. Guidance includes Reported Sales Growth of 7.0–8.0%, Operational Sales Growth of 7.5–8.5%, and Adjusted Operational Sales Growth of 6.2–7.2% (excluding the COVID-19 vaccine). The company projects Adjusted Reported EPS of $10.00–$10.10 (12.5% growth at midpoint) and Adjusted Operational EPS of $9.90–$10.00 (11.5% growth at midpoint). J&J reduced its share count by ~191 million, with a partial-year EPS benefit of ~$0.28 from ~73.5 million shares, secured $13.2 billion in cash from Kenvue’s debt offering and IPO, and retains a 9.5% Kenvue equity stake. The Consumer Health business will be reported as discontinued operations with an expected ~\$20 billion Q3 2023 gain. The company maintains its $1.19 quarterly dividend and has posted an investor webinar; all figures are recast for continuing operations.

Separation
•Company expects increased 2023 Reported Sales Growth of 7.0% - 8.0%, Operational Sales Growth of 7.5% - 8.5%, and
Adjusted Operational Sales Growth of 6.2% - 7.2%; Figures exclude the COVID-19 Vaccine
•Company expects 2023 Adjusted Reported Earnings Per Share (EPS) of $10.00 - $10.10, reflecting increased growth of

point
•Company reduced outstanding share count by approximately 191 million; 2023 guidance reflects only a partial-year benefit
of approximately 73.5 million shares or $0.28 benefit to EPS
•Company secured $13.2 billion in cash proceeds from the Kenvue debt offering and initial public offering and maintains 9.5%
of equity stake in Kenvue
•Company maintains its quarterly dividend of $1.19 per share
New Brunswick, N.J. (August 30, 2023) – Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) (“the Company”) today announced updates to its financials and
2023 guidance which reflect its operations as a company focused on transformational innovation in Pharmaceutical and MedTech. The
Company has published a recorded webinar for investors to provide additional context behind the updated financials and 2023 guidance
found in this release, which may be accessed by visiting the Investors section of the Company's website at webcasts & presentations.
“The completion of this transaction uniquely positions Johnson & Johnson as a Pharmaceutical and MedTech company focused on delivering
transformative healthcare solutions to patients,” said Joaquin Duato, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer. “We are incredibly
proud of the focus and dedication of our employees worldwide to achieve this milestone, which we are confident will unlock near- and long-
term value for all of our stakeholders.”
As previously announced, the Company recently completed an exchange offer to finalize the separation of Kenvue Inc., formerly Johnson &
Johnson’s Consumer Health business. As a result of the completion of the exchange offer, Johnson & Johnson will now present its
Consumer Health business financial results as discontinued operations, including a gain of approximately $20 billion in the third quarter of
2023.
Unless otherwise noted, the financial results and earnings guidance included below have been recast to reflect the continuing operations of
Johnson & Johnson.

top5_chunks.title: Adjusted Operational Sales Growth
top5_chunks.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Johnson & Johnson presents reconciliations between GAAP and non-GAAP metrics, explaining and quantifying adjustments to derive “Adjusted operational sales growth” and “Adjusted income before tax/net earnings from continuing operations,” along with rationale and limitations of these non-GAAP measures.

- Adjusted Operational Sales Growth (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Breakout by World Wide (WW), U.S., and International across Q1, Q2, first six months, Q3, first nine months, Q4, and full year.
  - Separates the effects of translational currency and acquisitions/divestitures (including a small Abiomed impact) from reported sales to show operational growth.
  - Key takeaways:
    - WW operational growth remained strong through most of 2022: ~9.1% in H1, ~8.9% through nine months, 6.5% for the full year; Q4 operational growth was roughly flat.
    - U.S. operational growth steady at ~3–4% throughout.
    - International operational growth robust (≈14–15%) for most of the year, with a Q4 dip; heavy currency headwinds meaningfully reduced reported growth vs. operational, especially outside the U.S.

- Segment-level Non-GAAP reconciliations (Income Before Tax from Continuing Operations):
  - For Q1 2023, Q2 2023 (quarter and year-to-date), and each 2022 quarter (Q1–Q4) plus year-to-date and full-year 2022.
  - Reported income before tax and margins for Pharmaceutical, MedTech, and Unallocated, then itemized adjustments to arrive at adjusted income before tax and adjusted margins.
  - Common adjustments include:
    - Intangible asset amortization
    - In-process R&D impairments
    - Litigation-related charges/credits
    - (Loss)/gain on securities
    - Restructuring
    - Acquisition, integration, and divestiture-related items
    - Medical Device Regulation (MDR) costs
    - COVID-19 vaccine-related costs
  - Illustrative results:
    - Q1 2023 adjusted IBT: $7.5B (36.1% margin) vs. reported loss due to large litigation charge in Unallocated.
    - Q2 2023 adjusted IBT: $8.0B (37.2%); 2023 YTD adjusted IBT: $15.5B (36.6%).
    - Full-year 2022 adjusted IBT: $28.0B (35.0%) vs. reported $19.4B (24.2%).

- GAAP to Non-GAAP reconciliations of consolidated P&L line items:
  - Periods covered: 2023 Q1, Q2, and first half; 2022 Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, and full year.
  - Reconciles cost of products sold, selling/marketing/admin, R&D, other (income)/expense, interest, restructuring, IPR&D impairments, and taxes to arrive at adjusted net earnings from continuing operations.
  - Tax reconciliations include impacts of:
    - Consumer Health separation tax-related costs
    - Tax legislation and other tax-related items
  - Highlights the impact of large, discrete items (e.g., litigation charges, COVID-19 vaccine-related costs, MDR costs, and securities gains/losses) on GAAP results and how they are removed to reflect underlying operational performance.

- Explanatory note on non-GAAP measures:
  - Defines “Adjusted operational sales growth” as excluding currency and M&A effects.
  - States the intended use (enhance understanding of underlying performance, internal evaluation, planning/forecasting) and limitations (not a GAAP substitute; may reduce comparability to peers).

top5_chunks.title: UPDATED FULL-YEAR 2023 GUIDANCE:
top5_chunks.summary:
- Johnson & Johnson issues updated full-year 2023 guidance (August 2023) excluding Consumer Health, contrasted with prior July 2023 guidance that included Consumer Health (pre-Kenvue separation).
- Key August 2023 outlook (ex-Consumer Health):
  - Adjusted operational sales growth: 6.2%–7.2% (midpoint 6.7%).
  - Operational sales: $83.6B–$84.4B (midpoint $84.0B), up 7.5%–8.5%.
  - Reported sales: $83.2B–$84.0B (midpoint $83.6B), up 7.0%–8.0%.
  - Adjusted operational EPS (diluted): $9.90–$10.00 (midpoint $9.95), up 11.0%–12.0%.
  - Adjusted EPS (diluted): $10.00–$10.10 (midpoint $10.05), up 12.0%–13.0%.
  - Average diluted shares: ~2,557 million.
- July 2023 guidance (including Consumer Health) for comparison:
  - Operational sales: $99.3B–$100.3B (midpoint $99.8B), up 7.0%–8.0%.
  - Reported sales: $98.8B–$99.8B (midpoint $99.3B), up 6.5%–7.5%.
  - Adjusted operational sales growth: 6.0%–7.0% (midpoint 6.5%).
  - Adjusted operational EPS (diluted): $10.60–$10.70 (midpoint $10.65), up 4.5%–5.5%.
  - Adjusted EPS (diluted): $10.70–$10.80 (midpoint $10.75), up 5.5%–6.5%.
  - Average diluted shares: ~2,631 million.
- Kenvue separation and capital actions:
  - Share count reduced by ~191 million via exchange offer; weighted average reduction of ~73.5 million shares recognized from Aug 23, 2023, adding ~$0.28 to full-year 2023 adjusted diluted EPS.
  - Generated $13.2B in cash from Kenvue debt offering and IPO.
  - Retains a 9.5% stake in Kenvue subject to a 90-day lockup; potential tax-efficient monetization in the next year, with no obligation if market conditions aren’t supportive.
- Dividend: Company will maintain its quarterly dividend of $1.19 per share.
- Non-GAAP framework and limitations:
  - Company does not provide GAAP forward-looking measures due to unpredictability of legal outcomes, unusual items, and acquisition-related effects.
  - Definitions provided for operational/adjusted operational sales growth and adjusted EPS metrics; figures exclude currency translation, net impact of acquisitions/divestitures, intangible amortization, special items, and COVID-19 vaccine.
  - Reconciliations and supplementary financial schedules available in the Investors section (webcasts & presentations).
- Additional information:
  - A recorded investor webinar provides context on the updated financials and guidance.
  - Notes include illustrative Euro rate usage and share count methodology post-Kenvue exchange.
  - Company overview emphasizes J&J’s mission and role as a diversified healthcare leader.

top5_chunks.title: Johnson & Johnson Announces Updated Financials and 2023 Guidance Following Completion of the Kenvue Separation - Introduction
top5_chunks.summary: Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) announced updated 2023 guidance following completion of the Kenvue separation, repositioning J&J as a Pharmaceutical and MedTech company. Guidance includes Reported Sales Growth of 7.0–8.0%, Operational Sales Growth of 7.5–8.5%, and Adjusted Operational Sales Growth of 6.2–7.2% (excluding the COVID-19 vaccine). The company projects Adjusted Reported EPS of $10.00–$10.10 (12.5% growth at midpoint) and Adjusted Operational EPS of $9.90–$10.00 (11.5% growth at midpoint). J&J reduced its share count by ~191 million, with a partial-year EPS benefit of ~$0.28 from ~73.5 million shares, secured $13.2 billion in cash from Kenvue’s debt offering and IPO, and retains a 9.5% Kenvue equity stake. The Consumer Health business will be reported as discontinued operations with an expected ~\$20 billion Q3 2023 gain. The company maintains its $1.19 quarterly dividend and has posted an investor webinar; all figures are recast for continuing operations.
top5_chunks.text:
Johnson & Johnson Announces Updated Financials and 2023 Guidance Following Completion of the Kenvue
Separation
•Company expects increased 2023 Reported Sales Growth of 7.0% - 8.0%, Operational Sales Growth of 7.5% - 8.5%, and
Adjusted Operational Sales Growth of 6.2% - 7.2%; Figures exclude the COVID-19 Vaccine
•Company expects 2023 Adjusted Reported Earnings Per Share (EPS) of $10.00 - $10.10, reflecting increased growth of
12.5% at the mid-point and Adjusted Operational EPS of $9.90 - $10.00, reflecting increased growth of 11.5% at the mid-
point
•Company reduced outstanding share count by approximately 191 million; 2023 guidance reflects only a partial-year benefit
of approximately 73.5 million shares or $0.28 benefit to EPS
•Company secured $13.2 billion in cash proceeds from the Kenvue debt offering and initial public offering and maintains 9.5%
of equity stake in Kenvue
•Company maintains its quarterly dividend of $1.19 per share
New Brunswick, N.J. (August 30, 2023) – Johnson & Johnson (NYSE: JNJ) (“the Company”) today announced updates to its financials and
2023 guidance which reflect its operations as a company focused on transformational innovation in Pharmaceutical and MedTech. The
Company has published a recorded webinar for investors to provide additional context behind the updated financials and 2023 guidance
found in this release, which may be accessed by visiting the Investors section of the Company's website at webcasts & presentations.
“The completion of this transaction uniquely positions Johnson & Johnson as a Pharmaceutical and MedTech company focused on delivering
transformative healthcare solutions to patients,” said Joaquin Duato, Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer. “We are incredibly
proud of the focus and dedication of our employees worldwide to achieve this milestone, which we are confident will unlock near- and long-
term value for all of our stakeholders.”
As previously announced, the Company recently completed an exchange offer to finalize the separation of Kenvue Inc., formerly Johnson &
Johnson’s Consumer Health business. As a result of the completion of the exchange offer, Johnson & Johnson will now present its
Consumer Health business financial results as discontinued operations, including a gain of approximately $20 billion in the third quarter of
2023.
Unless otherwise noted, the financial results and earnings guidance included below have been recast to reflect the continuing operations of
Johnson & Johnson.

top5_chunks.title: Adjusted Operational Sales Growth
top5_chunks.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Johnson & Johnson presents reconciliations between GAAP and non-GAAP metrics, explaining and quantifying adjustments to derive “Adjusted operational sales growth” and “Adjusted income before tax/net earnings from continuing operations,” along with rationale and limitations of these non-GAAP measures.

- Adjusted Operational Sales Growth (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Breakout by World Wide (WW), U.S., and International across Q1, Q2, first six months, Q3, first nine months, Q4, and full year.
  - Separates the effects of translational currency and acquisitions/divestitures (including a small Abiomed impact) from reported sales to show operational growth.
  - Key takeaways:
    - WW operational growth remained strong through most of 2022: ~9.1% in H1, ~8.9% through nine months, 6.5% for the full year; Q4 operational growth was roughly flat.
    - U.S. operational growth steady at ~3–4% throughout.
    - International operational growth robust (≈14–15%) for most of the year, with a Q4 dip; heavy currency headwinds meaningfully reduced reported growth vs. operational, especially outside the U.S.

- Segment-level Non-GAAP reconciliations (Income Before Tax from Continuing Operations):
  - For Q1 2023, Q2 2023 (quarter and year-to-date), and each 2022 quarter (Q1–Q4) plus year-to-date and full-year 2022.
  - Reported income before tax and margins for Pharmaceutical, MedTech, and Unallocated, then itemized adjustments to arrive at adjusted income before tax and adjusted margins.
  - Common adjustments include:
    - Intangible asset amortization
    - In-process R&D impairments
    - Litigation-related charges/credits
    - (Loss)/gain on securities
    - Restructuring
    - Acquisition, integration, and divestiture-related items
    - Medical Device Regulation (MDR) costs
    - COVID-19 vaccine-related costs
  - Illustrative results:
    - Q1 2023 adjusted IBT: $7.5B (36.1% margin) vs. reported loss due to large litigation charge in Unallocated.
    - Q2 2023 adjusted IBT: $8.0B (37.2%); 2023 YTD adjusted IBT: $15.5B (36.6%).
    - Full-year 2022 adjusted IBT: $28.0B (35.0%) vs. reported $19.4B (24.2%).

- GAAP to Non-GAAP reconciliations of consolidated P&L line items:
  - Periods covered: 2023 Q1, Q2, and first half; 2022 Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, and full year.
  - Reconciles cost of products sold, selling/marketing/admin, R&D, other (income)/expense, interest, restructuring, IPR&D impairments, and taxes to arrive at adjusted net earnings from continuing operations.
  - Tax reconciliations include impacts of:
    - Consumer Health separation tax-related costs
    - Tax legislation and other tax-related items
  - Highlights the impact of large, discrete items (e.g., litigation charges, COVID-19 vaccine-related costs, MDR costs, and securities gains/losses) on GAAP results and how they are removed to reflect underlying operational performance.

- Explanatory note on non-GAAP measures:
  - Defines “Adjusted operational sales growth” as excluding currency and M&A effects.
  - States the intended use (enhance understanding of underlying performance, internal evaluation, planning/forecasting) and limitations (not a GAAP substitute; may reduce comparability to peers).

top1_chunks.title: Firmwide overview
top1_chunks.summary:
- Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for Q1 2021, highlighting selected information and advising readers to consult the full Form 10‑Q and 2020 Form 10‑K for complete context, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Firmwide financial results (Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020):
  - Net income $14.3B, up $11.4B; diluted EPS $4.50, up 477%.
  - Total net revenue $32.3B, up 14%; noninterest revenue up 40% on stronger CIB Markets, higher Investment Banking fees, and absence of prior‑year losses; net interest income down 11% due to lower rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.
  - Noninterest expense $18.7B, up 12%, reflecting higher volume/revenue‑related costs, continued investments, and a $550M contribution to the Firm’s Foundation.
  - Provision for credit losses a net benefit of $4.2B driven by $5.2B allowance reduction, versus an $8.3B expense in prior year tied to a $6.8B allowance build.
  - Pre‑provision profit $13.5B, up 18%.
  - Returns: ROE 23% and ROTCE 29% (up from 4% and 5%).
  - Book value per share $82.31 (up 8%); tangible book value per share $66.56 (up 10%).
- Credit quality and reserves:
  - Total allowance for credit losses $25.6B; allowance for loan losses to retained loans coverage ratio 2.42% (down from 2.95% in Q4 2020; up from 2.32% YoY).
  - Nonperforming assets $10.3B, up $3.2B YoY due to deterioration across multiple wholesale industries and COVID‑19 impacts on consumer loans; down $649M from Dec 31, 2020, on portfolio activity and upgrades (notably Oil & Gas and Individuals) and sales of certain CIB consumer nonaccrual loans at fair value.
- Balance sheet trends:
  - Average loans ~$1.0T, up 1%, with growth in AWM and CIB, partially offset by declines in CCB and CB; PPP originations contributed in CCB and CB.
  - Average deposits ~$2.2T, up 36%, reflecting significant inflows across LOBs primarily from government actions in response to COVID‑19.
- Liquidity and capital:
  - Average eligible HQLA ~$697B; unencumbered marketable securities ~$841B; total liquidity sources ~ $1.5T.
  - Capital ratios (reflecting Federal Reserve COVID‑19 relief and CECL transition): CET1 13.1%, Tier 1 15.0%, Total capital 17.2%.
- Notes:
  - Certain prior‑period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Comparisons are Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020 unless otherwise specified.
top1_chunks.text:
Firmwide overview 
JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.3 billion for 
the first quarter of 2021 , or $4.50 per share, on net 
revenue of $32.3 billion. The Firm reported ROE of 23% 
and ROTCE of 29%. The Firm's results for the first quarter 
of 2021 included a reduction in the allowance for credit 
losses of $5.2 billion  compared to an increase in the 
allowance for credit losses of $6.8 billion in the prior year , 
as well as a $550 million contribution to the Firm's 
Foundation.  
•Net income was $14.3 billion, up $11.4 billion.
•Total net revenue was up 14%. Noninterest revenue was 
$19.4 billion, up 40%,  predominantly driven by higher 
CIB Markets revenue, higher Investment Banking fees, 
and the absence of losses in Credit Adjustments and 
Other in CIB and markdowns on held-for-sale positions in 
the bridge financing portfolio in CIB and CB recorded in 
the prior year. Net interest income was $12.9 billion, 
down 11%, predominantly driven by the impact of lower 
rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.   •Noninterest expense was $18.7 billion, up 12%, 
predominantly driven by higher volume- and revenue-
related expense and continued investments in the 
businesses. The increase in expense also included a $550 
million contribution to the Firm's Foundation.
•The provision for credit losses was a net benefit of $4.2 
billion driven by net reducti ons in the allowance for credit 
losses of $5.2 billion, compared to an expense of $8.3 
billion in the prior year predominantly driven by net 
additions to the allowance for credit losses of $6.8 
billion.   
•The total allowance for credit losses was $ 25.6 billion at 
March 31, 2021.  The Firm had an allowance for loan 
losses to retained loans coverage ratio of 2.42%, 
compared with 2.95% in the fourth quarter of 2020, and 
2.32% in the prior year; the decrease from the fourth 
quarter of 2020 was driven by net reductions  in the 
allowance for loan losses.
•The Firm’s nonperforming assets totaled $10.3 billion at 
M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, an increase of $3.2 billion from the 
prior year, reflecting client credit deterioration across 
multiple industries, including Real Estate, in the 
wholesale portfolio; and in the consumer portfolio, loans 
placed on nonaccrual status related to the impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic.  In the first quarter of 2021, 
nonperforming assets decreased $649 million from 
December 31, 2020, driven by lower nonaccrual loans in 
the wholesale portfolio , reflecting the impact of net 
portfolio activity and select client upgrades in Oil & Gas 
and Individuals; and lower nonaccrual loans at fair value 
in the CIB consumer portfolio, due to sales.  
•Firmwide average loans of $1.0 trillion were up 1%, 
driven by higher loans in AWM and CIB, predominantly 
offset by lower loans in CCB and CB. The increase in loans 
also reflects l oans originated under the Paycheck 
Protection Program (“PPP”) in CCB and CB.
•Firmwide average deposits of $2.2 trillion were up 36%, 
reflecting significant inflows across the LOBs  primarily 
driven by the effect of certain government actions in 
response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
•As of March 31, 2021, the Firm had average eligible High 
Quality Liquid Assets (“HQLA”) of approximately $697 
billion and unencumbered marketable securities with a 
fair value of approximately $841 billion, resulting in 
approximately $1.5 trillion of liquidity sources. Refer to 
Liquidity Risk Management on pages 42-46  for additional 
information.

top5_chunks.title: Consolidated statements of income (unaudited) for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020
top5_chunks.summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unaudited consolidated statements of income and comprehensive income for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020.
- Revenue mix:
  - Noninterest revenue rose to $19.4B from $13.8B, driven by higher investment banking fees ($3.0B vs $1.9B), principal transactions ($6.5B vs $2.9B), asset management/administration/commissions ($5.0B vs $4.5B), mortgage fees ($0.7B vs $0.3B), and card income ($1.35B vs $1.0B); investment securities gains declined ($14M vs $233M); lending- and deposit-related fees were roughly flat.
  - Net interest income declined to $12.9B from $14.4B as interest income fell (partly offset by lower interest expense).
  - Total net revenue increased to $32.3B from $28.3B.
- Credit costs: Provision for credit losses was a $4.2B benefit in 2021 versus an $8.3B expense in 2020.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense increased to $18.7B from $16.8B, led by higher compensation ($10.6B vs $8.9B); other categories (occupancy, technology/communications/equipment, professional services, marketing, other) are detailed.
- Earnings:
  - Income before income tax: $17.7B vs $3.2B.
  - Income tax expense: $3.4B vs $0.3B.
  - Net income: $14.3B vs $2.9B; net income applicable to common stockholders: $13.9B vs $2.4B.
  - EPS: Basic $4.51 vs $0.79; Diluted $4.50 vs $0.78. Weighted-average diluted shares: 3,078.9M vs 3,100.7M.
  - Note that prior-period amounts were revised to conform with current presentation.
- Other comprehensive income (OCI), after tax:
  - 2021 showed a $6.9B OCI loss (vs $5.8B OCI gain in 2020), reflecting losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, a DVA loss (vs prior-year gain), and smaller movements in translation adjustments, fair value hedges, and pension/OPEB.
- Comprehensive income:
  - $7.4B in 2021 vs $8.7B in 2020 (higher net income in 2021 offset by negative OCI).
- Notes to the unaudited consolidated financial statements are referenced as integral to the statements.

top5_chunks.title: INTRODUCTION
top5_chunks.summary:
- Introduces JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s MD&A for the first quarter of 2021, to be read alongside the 2020 Form 10-K and supported by a glossary and LOB metrics.
- Notes inclusion of forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with cross-references to related disclosures in this Form 10-Q and the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Provides a firm overview: a Delaware-incorporated (1968) U.S.-based global financial services leader with $3.7 trillion in assets and $280.7 billion in stockholders’ equity as of March 31, 2021, serving consumers, small businesses, and major corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Describes organizational structure and key entities: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 38 states and D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; and principal non-U.S. operating subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.).
- Outlines management reporting segments: four major reportable businesses—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment, with references to notes for detailed segment descriptions.
- Highlights investor communications and access: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) made available free on the firm’s website shortly after filing, with additional information via the Investor Relations site.
top5_chunks.text:
INTRODUCTION
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the first  quarter of 2021 . 
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the first  quarter of 
2021  (“Form 10-Q”) should be read together with JPMorgan 
Chase’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
December 31, 2020  (“2020  Form 10-K”). Refer to the 
Glossary of terms and acronyms and line of business (“LOB”) 
metrics on pages 163-171  for definitions of terms and 
acronyms used throughout this Form 10-Q.
The MD&A c ontains forward-looking statements within the 
meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 
1995. These forward-looking statements are based on the 
current beliefs and expectations of JPMorgan Chase’s 
management, speak only as of the date of this Form 10-Q and 
are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Refer to 
Forward-looking Statements on page 78  of this Form 10-Q, 
Part II, Item 1A, Risk Factors on pages 172-173  of this Form 
10-Q and Part I, Item 1A, Risk factors, on pages 8-32 of the 
2020  Form 10-K for a discussion of certain of those risks and 
uncertainties and the factors that could cause JPMorgan 
Chase’s actual results to differ materially because of those 
risks and uncertainties.
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding 
company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a 
leading  financial services firm based in the United States of 
America  (“U.S. ”), with operations worldwide.  JPMorgan 
Chase had  $3.7 trillion  in assets and $280.7 billion  in 
stockholders’ equity as of M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. The Firm is a 
leader in investment banking, financial services for 
consumers and small businesses, commercial  banking, 
financial transaction processing and asset management. 
Under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, the Firm serves 
millions of customers in the U.S. and globally many of the 
world’s most prominent corporate, institutional and 
government clients.  JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank , 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in  
38 states and Washington, D.C. as of  M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1. 
JPMorgan Chase’s principal non-bank subsidiary is J.P. 
Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. Morgan Securities”), a U.S. 
broker-dealer. The bank and non-bank subsidiaries of 
JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as well as through 
overseas branches and subsidiaries, representative offices 
and subsidiary foreign banks. The Firm’s principal operating 
subsidiary outside the U.S.  is J.P. Morgan Securities plc, a 
U.K.-based subsidiary of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.  
For management reporting purposes, the Firm’s activities 
are organized into four major reportable business 
segments, as well as a Corporate segment. The Firm’s 
consumer business segment is Consumer & Community 
Banking ( “CCB ”). The Firm’s wholesale business segments 
are the Corporate & Investment Bank ( “CIB”), Commercial 
Banking ( “CB”), and Asset & Wealth Management ( “AWM ”). 
Refer to Note 25 of this Form 10-Q and Note 32 of 
JPMorgan Chase’s 2020  Form 10-K for a description of the 
Firm’s business segments and the products and services 
they provide to their respective client bases.
The Firm's website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes important information about the Firm available on 
its website, including the Investor Relations section of its 
website at https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir.

Tangible book value per share (TBVPS) ended Q1 2021 at $66.56, up 10% year-over-year. Notes that pre-provision profit, ROTCE, and TBVPS are non-GAAP measures with reconciliations referenced.
- Business segment performance (Q1 2021):
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): ROE 54%; average deposits up 32%; client investment assets up 44%; average loans down 7%; card sales volume up 9%; active mobile customers up 9%.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): ROE 27%; 9.0% global investment banking wallet share; Total Markets revenue $9.1B, up 25% (Fixed Income up 15%, Equity up 47%).
  - Commercial Banking (CB): ROE 19%; gross investment banking revenue $1.1B, up 65%; average loans down 2%; average deposits up 54%.
  - Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): ROE 35%; AUM $2.8T, up 28%; average loans up 18%; average deposits up 43%.
- Credit provision and capital raising (first three months of 2021): $804B total credit provided and capital raised (excluding PPP loans), including $69B to consumers, $4B to U.S. small businesses, $300B to corporations, $417B capital raised for corporate clients and non-U.S. government entities, and $14B for nonprofits and U.S. government entities; plus $10B in PPP loans.
- References to additional details: non-GAAP reconciliations (pages 16–17) and business segment results (pages 18–34).

Firmwide overview 
JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.3 billion for 
the first quarter of 2021 , or $4.50 per share, on net 
revenue of $32.3 billion. The Firm reported ROE of 23% 
and ROTCE of 29%. The Firm's results for the first quarter 
of 2021 included a reduction in the allowance for credit 
losses of $5.2 billion  compared to an increase in the 
allowance for credit losses of $6.8 billion in the prior year , 
as well as a $550 million contribution to the Firm's 
Foundation.  
•Net income was $14.3 billion, up $11.4 billion.
•Total net revenue was up 14%. Noninterest revenue was 
$19.4 billion, up 40%,  predominantly driven by higher 
CIB Markets revenue, higher Investment Banking fees, 
and the absence of losses in Credit Adjustments and 
Other in CIB and markdowns on held-for-sale positions in 
the bridge financing portfolio in CIB and CB recorded in 
the prior year. Net interest income was $12.9 billion, 
down 11%, predominantly driven by the impact of lower 
rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.   •Noninterest expense was $18.7 billion, up 12%, 
predominantly driven by higher volume- and revenue-
related expense and continued investments in the 
businesses. The increase in expense also included a $550 
million contribution to the Firm's Foundation.
•The provision for credit losses was a net benefit of $4.2 
billion driven by net reducti ons in the allowance for credit 
losses of $5.2 billion, compared to an expense of $8.3 
billion in the prior year predominantly driven by net 
additions to the allowance for credit losses of $6.8 
billion.   
•The total allowance for credit losses was $ 25.6 billion at 
March 31, 2021.  The Firm had an allowance for loan 
losses to retained loans coverage ratio of 2.42%, 
compared with 2.95% in the fourth quarter of 2020, and 
2.32% in the prior year; the decrease from the fourth 
quarter of 2020 was driven by net reductions  in the 
allowance for loan losses.
•The Firm’s nonperforming assets totaled $10.3 billion at 
M a r c h   3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, an increase of $3.2 billion from the 
prior year, reflecting client credit deterioration across 
multiple industries, including Real Estate, in the 
wholesale portfolio; and in the consumer portfolio, loans 
placed on nonaccrual status related to the impact of the 
COVID-19 pandemic.  In the first quarter of 2021, 
nonperforming assets decreased $649 million from 
December 31, 2020, driven by lower nonaccrual loans in 
the wholesale portfolio , reflecting the impact of net 
portfolio activity and select client upgrades in Oil & Gas 
and Individuals; and lower nonaccrual loans at fair value 
in the CIB consumer portfolio, due to sales.  
•Firmwide average loans of $1.0 trillion were up 1%, 
driven by higher loans in AWM and CIB, predominantly 
offset by lower loans in CCB and CB. The increase in loans 
also reflects l oans originated under the Paycheck 
Protection Program (“PPP”) in CCB and CB.
•Firmwide average deposits of $2.2 trillion were up 36%, 
reflecting significant inflows across the LOBs  primarily 
driven by the effect of certain government actions in 
response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
•As of March 31, 2021, the Firm had average eligible High 
Quality Liquid Assets (“HQLA”) of approximately $697 
billion and unencumbered marketable securities with a 
fair value of approximately $841 billion, resulting in 
approximately $1.5 trillion of liquidity sources. Refer to 
Liquidity Risk Management on pages 42-46  for additional 
information.

- Document type and scope: Unaudited consolidated statement of income for JPMorgan Chase & Co. covering the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020, with amounts in millions (except per-share data).

- Credit costs: Large reserve release/negative provision for credit losses of $(4.2)B in 2021 versus an $8.3B provision in 2020.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense rose to $18.7B from $16.8B, driven mainly by higher compensation; occupancy, technology, professional services, and other costs detailed.
- Profitability:
  - Income before tax jumped to $17.7B from $3.2B; income tax expense increased to $3.4B from $0.3B.
  - Net income surged to $14.3B from $2.9B; net income applicable to common stockholders was $13.9B vs $2.4B.
- Earnings per share and shares:
  - Basic EPS $4.51 vs $0.79; diluted EPS $4.50 vs $0.78.
  - Slightly lower weighted-average shares outstanding year over year.
- Notes: Prior-period amounts revised to conform with current presentation; notes to the financial statements are integral to the statements.

top1_chunks.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the second quarter of 2023; directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and 2022 Form 10‑K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Headline results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income up 67% to $14.5B; EPS $4.75; ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Revenue: total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B, driven by:
  - Net interest income up 44% to $21.8B on higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; NII excluding Markets up 63% to $22.4B.
  - Noninterest revenue up 25% to $19.5B, reflecting the First Republic bargain purchase gain of ~$2.7B (Corporate) and stronger Markets NIR, partially offset by ~$900M of investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO.
  - Markets revenue declined, with lower Markets NII largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: noninterest expense up 11% to $20.8B, driven by higher compensation (headcount and wage inflation), ~$599M of First Republic–related expense, increased technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit costs: provision for credit losses of $2.9B, including a $1.5B net ACL build and $1.4B of net charge-offs.
  - ACL build includes ~$1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and commitments; additional builds in Card Services and wholesale (CB) largely offset by a reduction in Corporate.
  - Net charge-offs rose, mainly in Card, as 30+ day delinquencies normalized to pre‑pandemic levels.
- Allowance and asset quality: total ACL $24.3B; allowance-to-loans coverage ratio 1.75% (vs. 1.69% prior year); nonperforming assets ~$7.8B, flat year-over-year with mix shift toward wholesale nonaccruals.
- Balance sheet trends: firmwide average loans up 13% to ~$1.2T (CCB and CB, including First Republic); firmwide average deposits down 6% to ~$2.4T due to AWM migration to higher‑yielding investments, attrition in CIB/CB (including deliberate reductions), and higher CCB spending, partially offset by First Republic inflows in CCB and Corporate increases tied to international consumer initiatives.
- Capital and liquidity:
  - CET1 capital ~$236B; Standardized CET1 ratio 13.8% and Advanced CET1 ratio 13.9% (reflecting CECL transition); Tier 1 15.4%; Total capital 17.3%; SLR 5.8%.
  - Tangible book value per share $79.90 (up 15%); book value per share $98.11 (up 14%).
  - Liquidity: HQLA ~$792B and unencumbered marketable securities ~$620B, totaling ~ $1.4T of liquidity sources.
- Additional context:
  - Pre-provision profit up 71% to $20.5B.
  - Managed basis total net revenue $42.4B; Markets revenue $7.0B; memo metrics provided for NII/NIR excluding Markets.

Firmwide overview 
For the second  quarter of 2023 , JPMorgan Chase reported 
net income of $14.5 billion, up 67%, earnings per share of 
$4.75, ROE of 20% and ROTCE of 25% . The Fi rm's results 
for the second quarter of 2023 included an estimated 
bargain purchase gain of $2.7 billion in Corporate and a net 
addition to the allowance for credit losses of $1.2 billion 
associated with the First Republic acquisition. The Firm's 
results also included investment securities losses of $900 
million in Treasury and CIO. 
•Total net revenue  was $41.3 billion, up 34%, reflecting:
–Net interest income of $21.8 billion, up 44%, driven by 
higher rates and,  to a lesser extent, t he impact of the 
First Republic acquisition, partially offset by lower 
Markets net interest income and lower average deposit balances. Net interest income excluding Markets was 
$22.4 billion, up 63%.
–Noninterest revenue was $19.5 billion, up 25%, driven 
by the impact of the First Republic acquisition, higher 
Markets non interest revenue and the absence of losses 
on equity investments in Payments in the prior year, 
partially offset by higher net investment securities 
losses in Treasury and CIO. The impact of the First 
Republic acquisition included a $2.7 billion estimated 
bargain purchase gain in Corporate. 
–Total Markets revenue declined reflecting lower 
Markets NII, largely offset by higher NIR.
•Noninterest expense  was $20.8 billion, up 11%, driven 
by higher compensation expense due to additional 
headcount and the impact of wage inflation, $599 million 
expense associated with  the First Republic acquisition, 
higher technology and marketing investments and higher 
legal expense.
5•The provision for credit losses  was $2.9 billion, 
reflecting a $1.5 billion net addition to the allowance for 
credit losses and $1.4 billion of net charge-offs. The net 
addition to the allowance for credit losses included $1.2 
billion to establish the allowance for the First Republic 
loans and lending-related commitments. The net addition 
also reflected:
–$233 million in consumer predominantly in  Card 
Services, and
–$79 million in  wholesale reflecting $389 million in CB, 
largely offset by a $243 million reduction in Corporat e.
Net charge-offs increased $754 million, predominantly 
driven by CCB, primarily Card Services , as 30+ day 
delinquencies have returned to pre-pandemic levels. 
The prior year included a $428 million net addition to the 
allowance for credit losses and net charge-offs of $657 
million.
•The total allowance for credit losses  was $ 24.3 billion at 
June 30, 2023. The Firm had an allowance for loan losses 
to retained loans coverage ratio of 1.75%, compared 
with 1.69% in the prior year.
•The Firm’s nonperforming assets  totaled $7.8 billion at 
June 30, 2023, relatively flat from the prior year, as 
lower consumer nonaccrual loans due to loan sales in the 
prior year were offset by higher wholesale nonaccrual 
loans, reflecting client-specif ic downgrades . Refer to 
Wholesale Credit Portfolio on pages 70-79  for additional 
information.
•Firmwide  average loans  of $1.2 trillion were up 13%, 
driven by higher loans in CCB and CB, largely as a result  
of the First Republic acquisition. 
•Firmwid e average deposits  of $2.4 trillion were down 
6%, driven by: 
–the continued migration into higher-yielding 
investments in AWM; declines in CIB and CB primarily 
due to continued deposit attrition, which for CIB 
included actions to reduce certain deposits; and  a net 
decline in CCB primarily f rom existing accounts due to 
increased customer spending,
partially offset by
–the impact of the First Republic acquisition  in CCB, and 
an increase in Corporate related to the Firm's 
international consumer initiatives.
Refer to Liquidity Risk Management on pages 54-61  for 
additional information.

- Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): ROE 38%; average deposits down 2%; client investment assets up 42%; average loans up 19% YoY and 15% QoQ; Card Services net charge-off rate 2.41%; debit/credit card sales volume up 7% (ex-Commercial Card); active mobile customers up 10% (90-day active users; excludes First Republic impact as of June 30, 2023).

- Credit provided and capital raised (1H23): $1.2T total (loans and commitments), including $120B to consumers, $17B to U.S. small businesses, $520B to corporations, $535B capital raised for corporate clients and non-U.S. government entities, and $24B for nonprofit and U.S. government entities (states, municipalities, hospitals, universities).
- Reference: Further detail available in Business Segment Results (pages 22–46).

INTRODUCTION
The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the 
financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for 
the second  quarter of 2023 . 
This Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the second  quarter of 
2023  (“Form 10-Q”) should be read together with JPMorgan 
Chase’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
December 31, 2022  (“2022  Form 10-K”). Refer to the 
Glossary of terms and acronyms and line of business metrics 
on pages 200–208  for definitions of terms and acronyms used 
throughout this Form 10-Q.
This Form 10-Q contains forward-looking statements within 
the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 
1995. These forward-looking statements are based on the 
current beliefs and expectations of JPMorgan Chase’s 
management, speak only as of the date of this Form 10-Q and 
are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Refer to 
Forward-looking Statements on page 95 of this Form 10-Q; 
Part I, Item 1A, Risk Factors on pages 9-32  of the 2022  Form 
10-K; and Part II, Item 1A, Risk Factors on page 209  of this 
Form 10-Q for a discussion of certain of those risks and 
uncertainties and the factors that could cause JPMorgan 
Chase’s actual results to differ materially because of those 
risks and uncertainties. There is no assurance that actual 
results will be in line with any outlook information set forth 
herein, and the Firm does not undertake to update any 
forward-looking statements.
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (NYSE: JPM), a financial holding 
company incorporated under Delaware law in 1968, is a 
leading financial services firm based in the United States of 
America  (“U.S.”) , with operations worldwide. JPMorgan 
Chase had $3.9 trillion  in assets and $312.5 billion  in 
stockholders’ equity as of J u n e  3 0 ,  2 0 2 3. The Firm is a 
leader in investment banking, financial services for 
consumers and small businesses, commercial banking, 
financial transaction processing and asset management. 
Under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, the Firm serves 
millions of customers, predominantly in the U.S., and many 
of the world’s most prominent corporate, institutional and 
government clients  globally.  
JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in 
48 states and Washington, D.C.  JPMorgan Chase’s principal 
non-bank subsidiary is J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. 
Morgan Securities”), a U.S. broker-dealer. The bank and non-
bank subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as 
well as through overseas branches and subsidiaries, 
representative offices and subsidiary foreign banks. The 
Firm’s principal operating subsidiaries outside the U.S. are 
J.P. Morgan Securities plc and J.P. Morgan SE (“JPMSE”), 
which are subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and are 
based in the United Kingdom (“U.K.”) and Germany, 
respectively.For management reporting purposes, the Firm’s activities are 
organized into four major reportable business segments, as 
well as a Corporate segment. The Firm’s consumer business 
segment is Consumer & Community Banking (“CCB”). The 
Firm’s wholesale business segments are the Corporate & 
Investment Bank (“CIB”), Commercial Banking (“CB”), and 
Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”). Refer to Business 
Segment Results on pages 22-46  and Note 27 of this Form 
10-Q, and Note 32 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2022  Form 10-K, for 
a description of the Firm’s business segments and the 
products and services they provide to their respective client 
bases. On May 1, 2023, JPMorgan Chase acquired certain 
assets and assumed certain liabilities of First Republic Bank 
(the “First Republic acquisition”) from the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”).  Refer to Note 28 for 
additional information .
The Firm's website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes new and important information about the Firm 
available on its website at https://www.jpmorganchase.com, 
including on the Investor Relations section of its website at 
https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir. Information on the 
Firm's website is not incorporated by reference into this 
Form 10-Q or the Firm’s other filings with the SEC.

top5_chunks.title: Consolidated statements of income (unaudited) for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020
top5_chunks.summary:
- Presents JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unaudited consolidated statements of income and comprehensive income for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020.
- Revenue mix:
  - Noninterest revenue rose to $19.4B from $13.8B, driven by higher investment banking fees ($3.0B vs $1.9B), principal transactions ($6.5B vs $2.9B), asset management/administration/commissions ($5.0B vs $4.5B), mortgage fees ($0.7B vs $0.3B), and card income ($1.35B vs $1.0B); investment securities gains declined ($14M vs $233M); lending- and deposit-related fees were roughly flat.
  - Net interest income declined to $12.9B from $14.4B as interest income fell (partly offset by lower interest expense).
  - Total net revenue increased to $32.3B from $28.3B.
- Credit costs: Provision for credit losses was a $4.2B benefit in 2021 versus an $8.3B expense in 2020.
- Expenses: Noninterest expense increased to $18.7B from $16.8B, led by higher compensation ($10.6B vs $8.9B); other categories (occupancy, technology/communications/equipment, professional services, marketing, other) are detailed.
- Earnings:
  - Income before income tax: $17.7B vs $3.2B.
  - Income tax expense: $3.4B vs $0.3B.
  - Net income: $14.3B vs $2.9B; net income applicable to common stockholders: $13.9B vs $2.4B.
  - EPS: Basic $4.51 vs $0.79; Diluted $4.50 vs $0.78. Weighted-average diluted shares: 3,078.9M vs 3,100.7M.
  - Note that prior-period amounts were revised to conform with current presentation.
- Other comprehensive income (OCI), after tax:
  - 2021 showed a $6.9B OCI loss (vs $5.8B OCI gain in 2020), reflecting losses on investment securities and cash flow hedges, a DVA loss (vs prior-year gain), and smaller movements in translation adjustments, fair value hedges, and pension/OPEB.
- Comprehensive income:
  - $7.4B in 2021 vs $8.7B in 2020 (higher net income in 2021 offset by negative OCI).
- Notes to the unaudited consolidated financial statements are referenced as integral to the statements.

JPMorgan Chase  & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”), a

in 1968, is a leading global financial services firm in the

The accounting and financial reporting policies of  JPMorgan 
Chase  and its subsidiaries conform to  U.S. GAAP. 
Additionally, where applicable, the policies conform to the 
accounting and reporting guidelines prescribed by 
regulatory authorities.

in conformity with U.S. GAAP require management to make 
estimates and assumptions that affect the reported 
amounts of assets, liabilities, revenue and expense, and the 
disclosures of contingent assets and liabilities. Actual 
results could be different from these estimates. In the 
opinion of management, all normal, recurring adjustments 
have been included such that this interim financial 
information is fairly stated.

top1_chunks.title: Firmwide overview
top1_chunks.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for the second quarter of 2023; directs readers to the full Form 10‑Q and 2022 Form 10‑K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Headline results (Q2 2023 vs Q2 2022): net income up 67% to $14.5B; EPS $4.75; ROE 20%; ROTCE 25%.
- Revenue: total net revenue up 34% to $41.3B, driven by:
  - Net interest income up 44% to $21.8B on higher rates and, to a lesser extent, the First Republic acquisition; NII excluding Markets up 63% to $22.4B.
  - Noninterest revenue up 25% to $19.5B, reflecting the First Republic bargain purchase gain of ~$2.7B (Corporate) and stronger Markets NIR, partially offset by ~$900M of investment securities losses in Treasury and CIO.
  - Markets revenue declined, with lower Markets NII largely offset by higher Markets NIR.
- Expenses: noninterest expense up 11% to $20.8B, driven by higher compensation (headcount and wage inflation), ~$599M of First Republic–related expense, increased technology and marketing investments, and higher legal expense.
- Credit costs: provision for credit losses of $2.9B, including a $1.5B net ACL build and $1.4B of net charge-offs.
  - ACL build includes ~$1.2B to establish allowance for First Republic loans and commitments; additional builds in Card Services and wholesale (CB) largely offset by a reduction in Corporate.
  - Net charge-offs rose, mainly in Card, as 30+ day delinquencies normalized to pre‑pandemic levels.
- Allowance and asset quality: total ACL $24.3B; allowance-to-loans coverage ratio 1.75% (vs. 1.69% prior year); nonperforming assets ~$7.8B, flat year-over-year with mix shift toward wholesale nonaccruals.
- Balance sheet trends: firmwide average loans up 13% to ~$1.2T (CCB and CB, including First Republic); firmwide average deposits down 6% to ~$2.4T due to AWM migration to higher‑yielding investments, attrition in CIB/CB (including deliberate reductions), and higher CCB spending, partially offset by First Republic inflows in CCB and Corporate increases tied to international consumer initiatives.
- Capital and liquidity:

top5_chunks.title: Outlook
top5_chunks.summary:
- Regulatory updates: In July 2023, U.S. banking regulators proposed Basel III “finalization” changes replacing the advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach (no internal models except for Market risk) and applying the stress capital buffer to both expanded and standardized approaches. The rule would impact banks with assets of $100B+ (including U.S. GSIBs), with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2025 and a three-year transition. Separately, the Federal Reserve proposed revising the GSIB surcharge to an annual assessment based on averaged quarterly calculations (with daily averaging for certain inputs), reducing surcharge increments from 50 bps to 10 bps, and making technical Method 2 amendments, effective two quarters after finalization.

- Outlook and disclosures: The document contains forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with references to detailed risk factors and forward-looking statements sections. It notes that 2023 performance depends on macroeconomic, market, geopolitical, competitive, client activity, and regulatory developments, and that the firm will adjust operations as conditions evolve.

- FDIC special assessment: The FDIC proposed a special assessment (12.5 bps annual rate) on estimated uninsured deposits as of December 31, 2022, to recover DIF losses tied to March 12, 2023 systemic risk actions. If finalized as proposed, JPMorgan Chase expects to record approximately $3B pre-tax expense in the quarter of finalization, anticipated in 2H 2023.

- 2023 guidance: Management expects full-year net interest income and net interest income excluding Markets to be approximately $87B (market dependent), adjusted expense to be approximately $84.5B (market dependent and excluding any FDIC special assessment), and a Card Services net charge-off rate of about 2.6%. Certain figures are non-GAAP, with references to reconciliation pages.

top1_chunks.summary:
- Scope and purpose: MD&A for fiscal 2022 with comparisons to 2021; to be read with consolidated financial statements.
- Company overview: Global security and aerospace contractor focused on defense, space, intelligence, homeland security and IT/cyber; primary customer the U.S. Government. 2022 net sales mix: 73% U.S. Government (64% DoD), 26% international, 1% U.S. commercial. Four segments: Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space.
- Strategy and growth vectors: 21st Century Security vision to network platforms with open architectures; near/mid‑term growth from programs of record (e.g., F‑35 sustainment, PAC‑3, CH‑53K, Trident II D5), classified programs transitioning to production, hypersonics moving toward early production 2023–2026, and pursuit of new awards. Emphasis on tech investment, partnerships (including commercial), digital transformation, portfolio shaping, and disciplined capital allocation.
- Operating environment:
  - COVID‑19: Ongoing supply chain and labor disruptions into 2022; mitigation via $1.5B accelerated supplier payments and on‑site support; some impacts expected to continue into 2023.
  - Inflation/interest rates: Pressure on labor and supplier costs; risk to margins on fixed‑price contracts; pursuing EPA clauses and efficiencies; rising rates increase borrowing costs but reduce gross pension obligations.
  - Russia‑Ukraine conflict: Heightened demand (especially Europe) and U.S. stockpile replenishment; long-cycle nature tempers near-term sales impact; monitoring sanctions, supply chain, and elevated cyber threats.
- Portfolio and notable events:
  - Ongoing M&A/partnership evaluations.
  - UK renationalization of Atomic Weapons Establishment (AWE) effective June 30, 2021; 2021 had partial-year AWE results only.
- U.S. Government funding: FY23 Omnibus enacted $858B national defense ($816.7B DoD), plus $47B Ukraine supplemental (total $113B since March 2022). FY24 budget and debt ceiling debates introduce uncertainty; defense broadly expected to retain priority but program-level impacts unpredictable.
- International business: Strategy to grow international via FMS (74% of international sales) and DCS (26%). 2022 international sales concentration in Aeronautics, MFC, RMS. Ongoing demand for F‑35, F‑16, C‑130J; PAC‑3/THAAD; Aegis, surface combatants, training/logistics, and Sikorsky platforms.
- F‑35 program status: Strong international momentum (Finland, Switzerland, Germany; Canada selection); finalized LRIP Lots 15–17 for up to 398 aircraft; 2022 deliveries 141; cumulative deliveries 894. Late‑2022 GFE engine issue paused flight ops and deliveries; 2023 production targeted at 147–153 with 156/year targeted from 2025.
- Backlog: $150.0B at 12/31/22 (funded $95.5B), up from $135.4B; ~37% to be recognized within 12 months, ~61% within 24 months.
- Consolidated results (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Net sales: $66.0B, down 1.6% (products $55.5B, services $10.5B); supply chain headwinds weighed on volume.
  - Operating profit: $8.35B, down from $9.12B; gross profit down; RMS severance/impairment charges ($100M).
  - Interest expense up to $623M on new debt for share repurchases.
  - Non‑service FAS pension expense $971M, including $1.5B noncash settlement charge from pension risk transfer; 2021 included $1.7B settlement charge.
  - Other non‑operating swung to ($74M) from $288M on mark‑to‑market investment declines.
  - Effective tax rate 14.2% (R&D credits benefit). New tax rule to amortize R&D raised 2022 cash taxes by ~$660M; expected ~$575M in 2023. Inflation Reduction Act minimum tax/buyback excise expected immaterial.
  - Net earnings: $5.73B ($21.66/share) vs. $6.32B ($22.76); share count lower on buybacks.
- Segment performance (2022):
  - Aeronautics: Sales $27.0B (+1%); OP $2.87B (+2%); higher classified volume and F‑22 profit adjustments; F‑35 volume and net favorable adjustments lower; backlog up on Lot 15/16 awards.
  - MFC: Sales $11.3B (–3%); OP $1.64B (–1%); lower SOF GLSS and SNIPER volume; mixed IAMD (lower THAAD, lower PAC‑3 net favorable adjustments); tactical/strike mixed; backlog up on GMLRS and THAAD.
  - RMS: Sales $16.1B (–4%); OP $1.67B (–7%); lower TLS (non‑recurring 2021 pilot trainer), lower C6ISR and Black Hawk volume; higher CH‑53K; lower net favorable adjustments; backlog up on Sikorsky orders; FLRAA award protested.
  - Space: Sales $11.5B (–2%); OP $1.05B (–8%); AWE roll‑off; lower Orion; higher NGI and classified development; higher ULA equity earnings; lower net favorable adjustments; backlog up on Orion options and national security awards.
  - FAS/CAS pension operating adjustment $1.71B (favorable). Net profit booking rate adjustments added ~$1.8B to segment OP (down from ~$2.0B in 2021); includes ~$780M of unfavorable items.
  - Program risks: Canadian Maritime Helicopter (CH‑148) recovery depends on flight hours; potential contract restructuring. Turkish Utility Helicopter Program affected by U.S. sanctions; possible restructuring/termination.
- Liquidity and capital allocation:
  - Cash/cash equivalents $2.55B at year‑end.
  - Operating cash flow $7.80B (down from $9.22B) on timing (F‑35 production/billing, receivables, 2021 inventory liquidation non‑repeat) and supplier accelerations ($1.5B outstanding at YE).
  - Free cash flow $6.13B; capex $1.67B (facilities, equipment, IT).
  - Dividends $3.0B ($11.40/share); share repurchases $7.9B (18.3M shares), including $4.0B ASR; remaining buyback authorization $10B.
  - New debt: $2.3B issued May 2022 (used to redeem 2023/2025 notes and part of 2026); $4.0B issued Oct 2022 (to fund ASR). Total debt (net) $15.5B; ample credit facility/commercial paper access.
- Contractual commitments and guarantees:
  - Total contractual cash obligations ~$96.5B; purchase obligations include ~$53.7B tied to U.S. Government contracts (termination for convenience framework applies).
  - Offset obligations ~$16.1B notional through 2044; potential penalties ~$1.8B; mix of cash and non‑cash fulfillment.
  - Standby letters of credit/surety bonds/guarantees outstanding ~$3.75B total.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Long‑term contract revenue recognition predominantly over time via percentage‑of‑completion cost‑to‑cost; variable consideration, contract modifications, and profit booking rate adjustments can materially affect period results.
  - CAS vs. FAS pension accounting; favorable FAS/CAS operating adjustment when CAS exceeds FAS service cost.
- Postretirement benefit plans:
  - Continued pension de‑risking via group annuity purchases; 2022 transfer of $4.3B obligations/assets generated $1.5B settlement charge; cumulative transfers since 2018 ~$15.9B.
  - Key assumptions: discount rate 5.25% (up from 2.875%), expected long‑term asset return 6.5%; 2022 asset return ~–18%. ERISA funded status ~82% (ARPA impact); no 2022/2021 cash contributions.
  - CAS pension cost recoveries $1.8B in 2022; prepayment credits ~$4.3B at YE.
- Environmental matters: Recorded liabilities $696M; probable recoveries from U.S. Government pricing $618M; long‑duration remediation with periodic reassessment; most costs allowable under FAR.
- Goodwill and intangibles: Goodwill $10.8B; annual impairment testing found no impairments; Sikorsky goodwill (approx. $2.7B) and trademark considered at higher risk if cash flows deteriorate; no COVID‑19 or inflation‑driven impairments anticipated.
